Chapter 5
Methodology
Chapter abstract. This chapter details the eld wave, the calibration procedure,
and the in-silico procedure. It explains sampling, consent, ride context, the listening
episode, questionnaire blocks, the 60-to-52 screen, and quality checks. It then explains
the embedding, debiasing, manifold, persona, factorial ABM, and measurement steps,
with plain-language notes on each formal stage. It states the design limitations and
the analysis-plan discipline.
The empirical programme combines quantitative and qualitative eld mate-
rial, then distinguishes these human records from model-based evidence. The rst
is a measured eld wave, a cross-sectional questionnaire administered to university
students who listen to social media radio during rides with Uber, accompanied by 60
researcher-recorded qualitative case accounts. The questionnaire provides audience
and measurement summaries and supplies the target distribution for calibration.
The second is a calibrated in-silico experiment, a two-arm agent-based simulation
representing alternative platform congurations whose parameters were calibrated to
the measured wave, which supplies a model-conditional architectural counterfactual.
A further LLM-agent platform extension is specied but has not been conducted.
A separate synthesis of prototype FGD narratives informs prospective rule-based

and LLM-agent design without adding participants to the eld wave. This chapter
describes the evidence sources and their integration. Their separation is maintained
throughout: measured values are reported as measured, and simulated values are
reported as counterfactual estimates.
5.1
Ethical Protocol
The supplied F1.0 questionnaire states voluntary participation, academic use, the
option to skip items, and anonymous aggregate reporting. These are the instru-
ment's stated conditions, not proof of completed institutional approval. The sepa-
rate prole archive includes names and contextual descriptions; therefore the linked
research archive must be treated as identiable or pseudonymised rather than wholly
anonymous. This thesis reports only case codes and limited excerpts, not names,
detailed biographies, or trip traces.
The researcher must reconcile consent for linking notes to questionnaires
and for quoting recorded remarks with the original information given to students.
Permission for an academic questionnaire does not automatically authorise upload-
ing proles to an external LLM service. The planned agent extension requires a
separately approved data-use and de-identication procedure. Institutional autho-
risation is distinct from the consent wording and is not established by the statistical
les. No approval decision is inferred from the presence of data.

5.2
The Measured Study
5.2.1
Participants and Sampling
The target population was university students who listen to social media radio, in
Egypt, while riding with Uber in the October 6th City area, Giza. This venue was
chosen because it concentrates precisely the epistemic conditions the framework ad-
dresses: a bounded attention window, a social context, and exposure to broadcast
content through the drivers' or riders' devices. The planning calculation is docu-
mented in Appendix E; it is not evidence of power for an independent-groups eld
experiment.
A convenience sample of 60 respondents was recruited. The supplied form
asks respondents to consider a broadcast heard during a ride and explicitly excludes
ACU students. A seven-day eligibility window is not documented in that form and
is not imposed retrospectively. The historical analysis excluded eight records, leav-
ing N = 52 (30 male, 22 female). The analysis export contains six institutional
categories, with category counts of 3 to 13; no single category constitutes a majority
of the sample. All 52 records contribute to the pooled analyses. Identical answers
alone cannot establish that two records belong to the same person, so the exclusion
rule is a limitation as well as a data-processing step. The newly supplied process-
ing specication identies a 21-eld response-and-context key that reproduces the
retained sample (Section 6.4). The participant ow is shown in Figure 5.1.

5.2.2
Instrument
The analysed questionnaire batteries comprise 11 broadcaster-rating items and ve
post-broadcast items. The broadcaster battery contains four broadcast rigor (BR),
four social validation (SV), and three information quality (IQ) items. These 11 items
use 04 agreement responses; BR4 is reversed as 4 −BR4 before aggregation. PB1
PB5 address condence, perceived perspective diversity, comparative broadcaster
trust, structural clarity, and overall quality. Only PB uses 17 agreement responses.
The separate overall star rating uses a ve-point scale. Demographics, ride duration,
and self-reported interaction provide contextual variables.
The broader platform instrument bank also includes pre-broadcast, echo-
triggered, and weekly items. These are wider platform-design proposals, not the
eld questionnaire. Appendix A reproduces the supplied F1.0 stems and response
anchors, separating the administered form from prospective instruments. The sep-
arate star-rating block oers convergent self-report evidence, not an independent

factual-accuracy criterion.
5.2.3
Instrument Development
The supplied form makes the intended content and response anchors inspectable.
It does not provide an expert-panel voting matrix, cognitive-interview record, or
independent translation-validation study. Boateng et al. (2018) distinguish item
development, scale construction, and scale evaluation; evidence from one stage can-
not replace another. Here internal consistency and factor t assess properties of
the recorded responses, not completed content validation. The English and Arabic
wording is reproduced without claiming that the two versions have demonstrated
measurement equivalence.
PB3's comparative trust and PB4's structural clarity
must not be relabelled as verication intention and inuence of a displayed score.
The latter interpretations in earlier drafts did not match the supplied instrument.
5.2.4
Procedure
Respondents completed the questionnaire on a mobile device at the end of a so-
cial media radio listening episode during a ride. Completion followed the consent
screen.
The star rating and the PB battery were completed as separate blocks.
This separation does not eliminate common-source covariance, response styles, or
a general favourable impression (Podsako et al., 2024). The supplied les do not
establish exact administration timestamps or independently certify that every note
was recorded contemporaneously.

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY
86
5.2.5
The Ecological Momentary Assessment Schedule
The platform design species four measurement windows: pre-broadcast (PR1
PR3), post-broadcast (PB1PB5 and star rating), echo-triggered (EM1EM3), and
weekly (WK1WK15). The proposed post-broadcast trigger is within 30 seconds of
an episode ending, and the echo trigger is linked to the platform's diversity indica-
tor. These timing rules describe the intended EMA implementation, rather than a
longitudinal design completed by the 52-person survey. The supplied cross-sectional
exports do not contain session timestamps with which to assess compliance with a
30-second window. Accordingly, the present results are described as post-broadcast
questionnaire results, not as demonstrated longitudinal or real-time behavioural ef-
fects.
5.2.6
Analysis
Psychometric analysis used internal-consistency coecients (Cronbach's α and a
standardized one-factor model-based omega, exported as omega_bpa), corrected
item-total correlations with the specied retention oor of r ≥0.30, Spearman
associations with the separate, same-respondent star rating and with behaviourally
relevant covariates (ride duration, interaction level), and conrmatory factor anal-
ysis where the sample permitted. The small-sample strategy accepted exploratory
use of CFA with explicit reporting of t: the ve-item single-factor PB battery and
the eleven-item BRS were evaluated with t reported honestly, without assuming a
saturated solution before the N = 52 data were tted, and the single-factor result
is reported regardless of t. No completed invariance test is present in the supplied

87
exports. Group gures therefore describe observed scores, not comparable latent
means. Any later human latent-mean comparison would require a defensible mea-
surement structure and appropriate loading and intercept or threshold comparisons
(Putnick & Bornstein, 2016).
5.3
Mixed-Methods Design and Qualitative Corpus
The completed empirical report combines a quantitative questionnaire analysis with
a qualitative analysis of researcher-recorded ride encounters. Integration was under-
taken during this thesis revision, after the quantitative summaries were available; it
is not retrospectively described as a prospectively registered convergent design. The
purpose of mixing is complementarity and examination of tensions: what makes an
experience worthwhile, and when do numerical ratings or activity categories omit
that meaning? Creswell and Plano Clark (2018) and Levitt et al. (2018) motivate
specifying the purpose, timing, and point of integration rather than simply placing
two datasets side by side.
RQ5 (Qualitative experience). How do the rider records describe credi-
bility, listening value, participation, and platform experience? RQ6 (Integration).
Where do these accounts converge with, complement, or challenge the paired ques-
tionnaire ratings? These additional exploratory questions organise the newly inte-
grated analysis and are separate from the original H1H7 hypotheses.
The source corpus contains 60 case records in the rider-account corpus, with
observations, recorded remarks, and researcher reections, alongside duration,
mood, and interaction descriptors. All 60 have distinct identiers and nonempty

qualitative corpus: exclusion from a historical numeric analysis does not establish

treating them as independent samples.

5.3.1
Analytical Position and Coding Procedure
The analysis of the 60 rider records is a semantic, codebook-based thematic analysis,
with the assistance disclosed in the opening declaration, of recorded accounts. It is
informed by the distinctions among approaches to analysis discussed by Braun and
Clarke (2019), and by Kiger and Varpio's (2020) account of developing and reviewing
themes.
It is not described as independent human coding or a reliability-tested
content analysis of those records. A separate 193-segment FGD/self-report codebook
validation used three independent coders and is reported in Section 6.12.15.
The primary coding units were the key_observations and notable_quotes
elds. The researcher_reflections eld was read as interpretation, not counted
as independent participant testimony. Familiarisation distinguished observable ac-
tions, attributed remarks, and inferences about personality or platform success.

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY
89
Initial semantic codes concerned correction, source use, social endorsement, familiar
voices, calm, time t, agency, local relevance, and technical usability. These were
grouped into six themes, checked against the complete case inventory, and recorded
with an inclusion rule, exclusion rule, and case-level memo. A case could receive
multiple codes. Coding decisions are explicit in the case-level coding record; the
thematic codebook denes the themes, and Appendix F provides the membership
matrix.
The counts describe the reach of this coding within the supplied records;
they are not population prevalence estimates or measures of thematic importance.
The script joins codes to source identiers, calculates counts for 60 and 52 records,
and veries selected numerical summaries. It does not discover themes by keyword
frequency. For the 60 rider records, no second-coder agreement, member checking,
thematic saturation, or participant validation is claimed. The separate validation
provides coder agreement for the 25-code FGD/self-report codebook, not for the
rider-record themes. The audit retains source excerpts and interpretive decisions so
the analysis can be examined.
5.3.2
Integration and Qualitative Trustworthiness
A joint display combines selected case accounts with the same cases' PB scores
and interaction categories. It considers convergence, elaboration, and tension, not
whether each quotation conrms EST. Quiet appreciation, conditional preference,
and a request for better topic lters were retained rather than excluded as inconve-
nient cases. The small purposive illustrations do not support subgroup signicance
tests.

CHAPTER 5. METHODOLOGY
90
The records are polished, predominantly favourable English narratives with
recurrent links between academic discipline and media preference. That style limits
how closely they can be treated as spontaneous speech. The archive does not estab-
lish whether every attributed quotation is verbatim, translated, or reconstructed.
Excerpts are therefore identied as recorded remarks, not certied interview tran-
scripts. Positive descriptions cannot establish absence of dissatisfaction, and a re-
searcher's explanation of a student's motives is not direct access to that student's
experience. This is a complete analysis of the supplied case corpus, not a claim of
exhaustive understanding of the wider student population.
The questionnaire's promise of anonymity must be distinguished from the
identiable prole archive. Names and detailed backstories are not reproduced in
the results. Publication, retention, and later LLM processing require a consent and
access review. No prole data were sent to external model APIs for the proposed
experiment during this revision.
5.4
Focus-Group Evidence and Its Role in the Study
The prototype FGD is separate from the rider records in Section 5.3. Two overlap-
ping narratives describe one reported university wireframe walkthrough; they are
not two samples and are not added to the 60 rider accounts or 52 retained ques-
tionnaires. Participant overlap is unknown. Appendix G contains the full merged
report, codebook, recording audit, and interpretive limits.
The accounts describe Egyptian Arabic discussion, an ACU context, smart-
phone wireframes, and an approximately 28-minute session. The more precise re-

ported duration is 1,675.33 seconds, not metadata independently measured here.
The transcript, recording, roster, and consent documentation remain absent. The
analysis is consequently a critical synthesis of reported narratives, not newly com-
pleted transcript-level coding. Its four domains, FGD-T1FGD-T4, remain distinct
from the rider corpus's T1T6 codes.
A supplemental le, fgd_analysis_parts.json, supplies seven generated
text summaries, not an original transcript, frame log, or additional sample.
Its
candidate extracts contain translation inconsistencies, malformed intervals, and un-
certain speaker labels. The review accepts the existence of the export and retains
programme-length and registration-feedback questions for later source checking; it
does not accept claims that the primary records have been recovered. The decision
record is summarised in Appendix G.4. Model-use provenance is disclosed in the
opening declaration. No new inductive transcript coding or audiovisual triangula-
tion is claimed.
Focus groups require attention to interaction, not an assumption that a mod-
erator's explanation constitutes participant endorsement (Kitzinger, 1995). The syn-
thesis separates reported experience, interpretation, competing explanations, and
implications. No quotations, theme prevalence, saturation, or coding reliability are
invented. COREQ and APA qualitative reporting guidance inform the documenta-
tion checks without certifying missing procedures (Levitt et al., 2018; Tong et al.,
2007).

5.4.1
Empirical Anchors, Assumptions, and Factual Ground Truth
Empirical anchors are source-linked human accounts or observations used within
their evidentiary limits. Design assumptions are proposed mechanisms or scenario
settings. Factual ground truth refers more narrowly to independently adjudicated
answers for a dened assessment task. A preference for co-hosting is not a veried
answer to a news claim, and a theme is not an estimated transition probability.
The FGD currently supplies provisional design hypotheses, not veried indi-
vidual personas, numerical calibration targets, or factual answer keys. Its repeated
lexical counts are retained for audit only. New extracts must enter the evidence
register with locators, speaker roles, quotation/translation status, permission scope,
and coding decisions before participant-level use.

5.5
The Calibrated In-Silico Experiment (Final Pipeline)
The nal computational study is a calibrated in-silico experiment, not a eld in-
tervention. It has three stages: (1) four-stream embedding, machine-learning de-
biasing, and Monte-Carlo prior construction; (2) a within-persona 23 full-factorial
tensor agent-based model (ABM) with eight mathematical inuence lters and a
Zewail-inspired attentional gate; and (3) a GRM-IRT measurement model with
dual frequentist and Bayesian inference, adversarial stress tests, and global sen-
sitivity analysis. The complete implementation, data, seeds, and generated outputs
are included in the reproducibility archive (Appendix K).
The pipeline is deliberately explicit about what it can and cannot identify.
The measured wave anchors the prior and the measurement model. The architectural
contrast is a counterfactual generated within the model. No simulation output is
relabelled as a human treatment eect.

The empirical streams anchor the
persona distribution, the measurement model, and the semantic features. The treat-

−0.06 on engagement) are design assumptions. They are not estimated from the
52 respondents. The simulation propagates those assumptions through the ABM
and the measurement model; it does not identify a eld treatment eect. The value
of the exercise lies in the internal consistency of the implied design, the epistemic

Sentence-transformer architecture and process.
The encoder is BAAI/
bge-m3, a multilingual sentence-transformer built on an XLM-RoBERTa backbone.
It returns a 1,024-dimensional dense sentence vector and supports long inputs up
to 8,192 tokens.
The thesis uses the dense embedding only; the model's sparse
and multi-vector outputs are not used. The encoder is used zero-shot: it is not
ne-tuned on the thesis data, and no supervised label enters the embedding step.
The process is: (1) assemble the 5,258 document texts and their source metadata;
(2) clean and truncate each text to the model limit; (3) tokenise and encode
mini-batches on the Colab T4 in mixed precision; (4) pool and L2-normalise the
dense representation; (5) cache the vectors by a hash of the model name and
document set; and (6) project the semantic block to 32 principal components, which
enter the 198-feature matrix alongside the 31 quantitative features.
The cache
makes the run reproducible without a second API call.

5.5.3
Stage 1: Monte-Carlo Prior Q0 and Random Personas
A continuous prior Q0(θ) is tted to the debiased coordinates. When the sample
covariance is well conditioned, a Gaussian kernel density estimator is used; other-
wise a shrunken multivariate normal is substituted. The generator draws n = 500
personas, θa ∼Q0, and maps the six latent axes to the ABM traits (initial opinion,
prior reputation, echo susceptibility, heat capacity, critical scrutiny, and co-hosting
preference). Every persona is cloned across all eight factorial cells, so within-persona
contrasts are paired by construction. The n = 500 personas are a computational
population, not 500 additional human respondents.
Who the synthetic personas represent.
The personas are drawn after
DML/IPW and after the six-axis spectral projection, so they inherit the debiased
latent geometry of the 52 measured students, not the raw questionnaire rows. The
measured anchor is a convenience sample of university students who were Uber
riders in the October 6th City area, Giza: age mean 20.37 (SD 0.95; range 1923),
30 male and 22 female respondents, academic years 14, and eight faculties across
six universities. The ABM does not assign age, gender, or faculty to individual

respondent in the debiased manifold, for partial pooling only.
A descriptive
projection onto those nearest anchors gives approximately 268 male and 232 female

not a persona attribute and is not a representative demographic sample.

 IPW. Reweight the sample so the high-interaction group is not overrepre-

 PCA, LLE, and Laplacian eigenmaps. Compress 198 columns into six

 Q0 and personas. Fit a smooth distribution to the 52 debiased rows and

In plain terms: create plausible synthetic
listeners that sit inside the measured cloud, not 500 new humans.
 Factorial ABM. Test all eight on/o combinations in the same persona across
18 sessions.
In plain terms: compare the design bundles within the same
synthetic person, so dierences are not due to dierent people.
 GRM-IRT. Turn a latent score into item responses with thresholds. In plain

 Bayesian check. Fit a one-sample model to the paired dierences. In plain
